questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of chronic heart failure (EF = 35%) and hypertension presents to the emergency department with complaints of worsening shortness of breath and dizziness. He was recently started on a new medication for heart failure. On examination, his heart rate is 48 bpm, and his blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg. ECG shows sinus bradycardia without AV block. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bisoprolol

 

Beta-blockers like Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, and Metoprolol succinate are recommended for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) because they reduce mortality. However, they can cause bradycardia and hypotension, especially when started at a high dose or in patients with a low baseline heart rate.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Digoxin: Can cause bradycardia, but it is more commonly associated with AV block and arrhythmias rather than just sinus bradycardia.

 

Option C. Furosemide: A loop diuretic used for volume overload in CHF. It does not typically cause bradycardia, but it can lead to hypotension if overused.

 

Option D. Spironolactone: A potassium-sparing diuretic that reduces mortality in CHF. It does not directly cause bradycardia, though hyperkalemia-induced conduction abnormalities can occur.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with non-small cell lung cancer is receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy. His oncologist prescribes a combination of ondansetron, dexamethasone, and aprepitant for nausea and vomiting prevention. A few days later, the patient, who is also on warfarin for a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), undergoes routine INR monitoring, which reveals a significant drop in INR levels. Which of the following best explains the interaction between aprepitant and warfarin?

options.label: A
options.text: Aprepitant induces CYP2C9, increasing warfarin metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: Aprepitant inhibits CYP2C9, decreasing warfarin metabolism

options.label: C
options.text: Aprepitant induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism

options.label: D
options.text: Aprepitant inhibits CYP3A4, decreasing warfarin metabolism

questions.answerText: Aprepitant induces CYP2C9, increasing warfarin metabolism
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Aprepitant induces CYP2C9, increasing warfarin metabolism

 

Aprepitant is a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor and a weak CYP2C9 inducer. Since warfarin is primarily metabolized by CYP2C9, aprepitant induces its metabolism, leading to reduced warfarin levels and a drop in INR, increasing the risk of thrombosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Aprepitant inhibits CYP2C9, decreasing warfarin metabolism: Incorrect. If CYP2C9 were inhibited, warfarin levels would rise, causing increased INR and bleeding risk.

 

Option C. Aprepitant induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism: Incorrect. Aprepitant is not an inducer of CYP3A4; it is a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A4.

 

Option D. Aprepitant inhibits CYP3A4, decreasing warfarin metabolism: Incorrect. Warfarin is not primarily metabolized by CYP3A4, so this would not significantly affect its levels.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old hiker is brought to the emergency department by his friends after eating wild berries during a trek. He is agitated, confused, and hallucinating, attempting to grab imaginary objects in the air. His skin is dry and flushed, pupils are bilaterally dilated, and he has urinary retention. His heart rate is 120 bpm, and his temperature is 39.5°C (103°F). Which of the following drugs is the best treatment for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Physostigmine

 

This patient has anticholinergic toxicity, most likely from ingesting Dhatura or other plants containing belladonna alkaloids. The classic toxidrome includes:

 

  • Hallucinations, agitation, delirium ("mad as a hatter")
  • Dry, flushed skin ("red as a beet, dry as a bone")
  • Mydriasis with blurred vision ("blind as a bat")
  • Hyperthermia ("hot as a hare")
  • Urinary retention ("full as a flask")

 

Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, reverses anticholinergic toxicity by increasing acetylcholine levels, counteracting the muscarinic blockade.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Flumazenil: Used for benzodiazepine overdose, not effective in anticholinergic toxicity.

 

Option B. Naloxone: Used for opioid overdose, which presents with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression, not hyperthermia or hallucinations.

 

Option D. Diazepam: Can help with seizures or agitation, but does not reverse the underlying toxicity.

questions.stem: A woman at 8 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with hypothyroidism. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L-thyroxine

 

Pregnant women with hypothyroidism require L-thyroxine (levothyroxine) because:

 

  • Maternal hypothyroidism can lead to fetal neurodevelopmental defects, miscarriage, and preterm birth.
  • L-thyroxine is safe in pregnancy and mimics natural thyroid hormone (T4).
  • Dosage requirements increase during pregnancy due to higher thyroid hormone demand (estrogen-induced increase in thyroxine-binding globulin and placental deiodinase activity).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Methimazole: Incorrect. This is an antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

 

Option C. Propylthiouracil: Incorrect. Used for hyperthyroidism, particularly in the first trimester, not for hypothyroidism.

 

Option D. Radioactive iodine: Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as it destroys fetal thyroid tissue.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 35 weeks of gestation is receiving LMWH for a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) earlier in pregnancy. She presents to the hospital in early labor. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Switch to intravenous unfractionated heparin

 

Why?

 

  • LMWH has a long half-life (~12 hours) and is not easily reversible.
  • In late pregnancy (≥36 weeks), patients at high risk of thrombosis are typically switched from LMWH to unfractionated heparin (UFH) because:
    • UFH has a shorter half-life (~1-2 hours), allowing easier discontinuation before delivery.
    • It can be rapidly reversed with protamine sulfate, reducing the risk of excessive bleeding at delivery.
    • UFH is stopped 4-6 hours before delivery and restarted postpartum.

 

UFH provides better control before delivery, and can be stopped quickly if labor progresses.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Continue LMWH until delivery: Incorrect. LMWH has a long half-life, increasing the risk of bleeding complications during delivery.

 

Option C. Stop LMWH and induce labor: Incorrect. Stopping LMWH without a bridge increases thrombosis risk. Induction is not routinely needed unless obstetrically indicated.

 

Option D. Switch to warfarin immediately: Incorrect. Warfarin is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy, and should be started postpartum if long-term anticoagulation is needed.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes prostate surgery (TURP). During the procedure, he develops persistent bleeding due to excessive fibrinolysis. The surgeon decides to administer a medication to inhibit fibrinolysis and control bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tranexamic acid

 

Why?

 

  • TURP syndrome and postoperative bleeding are often due to excessive fibrinolysis, leading to clot breakdown.
  • Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic agent that blocks plasmin activation, preventing fibrin degradation and reducing bleeding.
  • TXA is commonly used in surgical bleeding, postpartum hemorrhage, and trauma to enhance clot stability.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alteplase: Incorrect. It is a thrombolytic agent (tPA) that activates plasminogen, increasing fibrinolysis and worsening bleeding.

 

Option C. Clopidogrel: Incorrect. It is an antiplatelet drug that prevents platelet aggregation and is not used for fibrinolysis-related bleeding.

 

Option D. Heparin: Incorrect. It is an anticoagulant that inhibits thrombin and factor Xa, increasing bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 presents with recurrent hyperkalemia on routine blood tests. He is currently on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. Which of the following diuretics would be the most appropriate choice for managing his hypertension?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Furosemide

 

Why?

 

  • The patient has CKD with recurrent hyperkalemia.
  • Loop diuretics like furosemide are preferred in CKD as they promote potassium excretion and help manage fluid overload.
  • Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) are ineffective in advanced CKD (GFR <30 mL/min).
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone) and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) are not suitable due to their effects on potassium balance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Spironolactone: Incorrect. Aldosterone antagonist, potassium-sparing, can worsen hyperkalemia, especially in CKD.

 

Option B. Hydrochlorothiazide: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretic, but less effective in CKD (GFR <30) and does not significantly lower potassium.

 

Option D. Acetazolamide: Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, causes bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis, and does not effectively manage hypertension or hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of Alzheimer’s disease presents with urinary urgency, frequency, and nocturia. He has had multiple episodes of urinary incontinence over the past few months. Digital rectal examination reveals a normal-sized prostate with no nodularity. Post-void residual urine is 20 mL (within normal range). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mirabegron

 

Why?

 

  • The patient has Overactive Bladder (OAB) rather than BPH, as evidenced by:
    • Storage symptoms (urgency, frequency, incontinence).
    • Normal prostate size on DRE.
    • Low post-void residual (20 mL), ruling out obstruction.
  • Mirabegron (β3-adrenergic agonist) is preferred because it does not have anticholinergic side effects, making it safer in dementia patients.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oxybutynin: Incorrect. Anticholinergic, can worsen cognitive decline in dementia.

 

Option C. Tamsulosin: Incorrect. Selective α1A-blocker, used for BPH with voiding symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream), but not for OAB.

 

Option D. Prazosin: Incorrect. Non-selective α1-blocker, used for hypertension and BPH but not preferred due to risk of postural hypotension.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with complaints of irritability, poor appetite, and abdominal pain. On examination, the child has pallor, cognitive delay, and a bluish line on the gums (Burton’s line). Blood investigations reveal a microcytic hypochromic anemia with a blood lead level of 75 µg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dimercaprol (BAL) + Calcium disodium EDTA

 

  • The child has severe lead poisoning (Blood lead level >70 µg/dL) with neurological symptoms (irritability, cognitive delay).
  • The standard treatment for severe lead poisoning is IM BAL followed by IV EDTA, as BAL prevents lead redistribution to the brain, and EDTA enhances renal excretion.

 

Management of Lead Poisoning

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Calcium disodium EDTA (CaNa₂EDTA) alone: Incorrect. Used in moderate cases (lead level 45-69 µg/dL) but not sufficient for severe poisoning.

 

Option C. Penicillamine: Incorrect. Used for mild cases but is not first-line in severe poisoning.

 

Option D. Deferoxamine: Incorrect. Used for iron poisoning, not lead.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of ischemic heart disease and a recent myocardial infarction develops ventricular tachycardia. He is given an intravenous loading dose of lignocaine followed by a maintenance infusion. Which of the following factors primarily determines the loading dose of lignocaine in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Volume of Distribution

 

  • Loading dose (LD) formula: LD = Vd × C target where Vd (Volume of Distribution) determines how much drug is needed to achieve the desired plasma concentration (C target).
  • Since lignocaine is administered IV, bioavailability (F) is irrelevant (F = 1 in IV drugs).
  • Clearance (Cl) and half-life (t½) influence maintenance dose, not the loading dose.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clearance: Determines the maintenance dose, not the loading dose.

 

Option C. Half-life: Affects dosing interval but not loading dose calculation.

 

Option D. Bioavailability: Relevant for oral drugs, but not for IV drugs like lignocaine.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old hypertensive male has been on an antihypertensive drug for several months. He reports persistent drowsiness, dry mouth, and lethargy but continued the medication. However, after forgetting to take it for 3 days, he presents to the ER with severe hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and anxiety. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his rebound hypertension?

options.label: A
options.text: Upregulation of α2-receptors in the CNS

options.label: B
options.text: Increased norepinephrine release due to loss of presynaptic inhibition

options.label: C
options.text: Reflex activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

options.label: D
options.text: Increased sensitivity of vascular smooth muscle to circulating catecholamines

questions.answerText: Increased norepinephrine release due to loss of presynaptic inhibition
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Increased norepinephrine release due to loss of presynaptic inhibition

 

  • The patient was most likely taking Clonidine, a centrally acting α2-agonist that inhibits sympathetic outflow.
  • Chronic use suppresses norepinephrine (NE) release via presynaptic α2-receptor activation.
  • Stopping clonidine suddenly → loss of presynaptic inhibition → excess NE release → severe rebound hypertension.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Upregulation of α2-receptors in the CNS: No evidence that α2-receptors significantly upregulate; the issue is NE overactivity.

 

Option C. Reflex activation of the RAAS: RAAS does play a role in hypertension, but not the primary cause of clonidine withdrawal crisis.

 

Option D. Increased sensitivity of vascular smooth muscle to circulating catecholamines: Seen in β-blocker withdrawal, not clonidine withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with dyslipidemia was started on a lipid-lowering drug. He later developed muscle pain, weakness, and dark-colored urine. His creatine kinase (CK) levels are markedly elevated, and his renal function is worsening. On history, he reports that he was recently prescribed erythromycin for a respiratory infection. Which of the following lipid-lowering drugs is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Atorvastatin

 

  • The patient has statin-induced rhabdomyolysis, worsened by erythromycin interaction.
  • Erythromycin (a macrolide) inhibits CYP3A4, which is responsible for statin metabolism, leading to increased statin levels and muscle toxicity.
  • Signs of rhabdomyolysis:
    • Severe muscle pain & weakness
    • Markedly elevated CK (>10× ULN)
    • Myoglobinuria (dark urine) → Acute kidney injury

 

Atorvastatin Metabolized by CYP3A4, levels rise with erythromycin → High risk of rhabdomyolysis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Colesevelam: A bile acid sequestrant; not affected by CYP3A4 and does not cause myopathy.

 

Option C. Ezetimibe: Inhibits cholesterol absorption; no CYP interaction, minimal muscle toxicity.

 

Option D. Alirocumab: A PCSK9 inhibitor; administered subcutaneously, not metabolized by CYP3A4, does not cause rhabdomyolysis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Statins + CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., erythromycin, clarithromycin, azoles, cyclosporine, amiodarone, grapefruit juice) = Increased risk of rhabdomyolysis.
  • Monitor CK levels in patients taking statins with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
  • Switch to statins less dependent on CYP3A4 (e.g., Rosuvastatin, Pravastatin) in high-risk patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs, when given with ketoconazole, can cause QT prolongation and Torsades’ de pointes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cisapride

 

Cisapride is the correct answer because it is a prokinetic agent that blocks hERG potassium channels, causing QT prolongation.

 

  • Cisapride is metabolized by CYP3A4.
  • Ketoconazole is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, leading to increased levels of cisapride.
  • This increases the risk of QT prolongation and Torsades de Pointes (TdP).
  • Cisapride was withdrawn from many markets due to this life-threatening risk.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cetirizine: Does not cause significant QT prolongation and has a better cardiac safety profile.

 

Option C. Loratadine: Loratadine is metabolized by CYP3A4 but has minimal effects on the QT interval.

 

Option D. Promethazine: While it is a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic effects, it does not significantly prolong the QT interval.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female with mild persistent asthma is prescribed an inhaled corticosteroid. She is concerned about potential side effects. Which of the following measures can help minimize the risk of local side effects from inhaled corticosteroids?

options.label: A
options.text: Using a high-dose inhaled corticosteroid from the start

options.label: B
options.text: Rinsing the mouth with water after inhalation

options.label: C
options.text: Using a systemic corticosteroid instead of an inhaled one

options.label: D
options.text: Taking the inhaled corticosteroid on an empty stomach

questions.answerText: Rinsing the mouth with water after inhalation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Rinsing the mouth with water after inhalation

 

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the mainstay for controlling persistent asthma, but they can cause local side effects such as oral candidiasis and dysphonia.

 

  • Prevents oropharyngeal deposition of the drug, reducing the risk of oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
  • Patients should also spit out the water instead of swallowing it.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A) Using a high-dose inhaled corticosteroid from the start: Incorrect. High doses increase the risk of systemic and local side effects without additional benefit in mild asthma. Asthma management follows a stepwise approach, starting with the lowest effective dose.

 

Option C. Using a systemic corticosteroid instead of an inhaled one: Incorrect. Systemic corticosteroids have more severe side effects (e.g., adrenal suppression, osteoporosis) and should be reserved for severe cases or exacerbations.

 

Option D. Taking the inhaled corticosteroid on an empty stomach: Incorrect.ICS act locally in the lungs, and their effect is unrelated to food intake.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Rinsing the mouth after ICS use prevents oropharyngeal candidiasis.
  • Use the lowest effective dose to minimize side effects.
  • A spacer device can also help reduce local side effects.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of inhibition from the given graph:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mixed Inhibition

 

In the given Lineweaver-Burk plot:

 

  • Both the slope and Y-intercept are different, indicating that Vmax is decreased (since Y-intercept = 1/Vmax).
  • The X-intercept is also altered, indicating that Km may increase or decrease depending on whether the inhibitor favors binding to the free enzyme or the enzyme-substrate complex.

 

These findings are characteristic of mixed inhibition, where the inhibitor can bind to both the free enzyme and the enzyme-substrate complex, but with different affinities.

 

Thus, the correct answer is (D) Mixed Inhibition.

questions.stem: In which phase of clinical trials is the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of a drug determined?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Phase 1

 

  • Phase 1 clinical trials primarily focus on drug safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in a small number of healthy volunteers or patients (if the drug is highly toxic, e.g., in oncology).
  • One of the key objectives is to determine the Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD) and the appropriate dosing range.
  • Escalating doses are given to different cohorts to assess dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) and establish a safe starting dose for later trials.

 

Other Phases:

 

Option B. Phase 2: Evaluates drug efficacy and optimal dosing in a larger patient group with the target disease.

 

Option C. Phase 3: Confirms efficacy and safety in a larger, diverse population before regulatory approval.

 

Option D. Phase 4: Post-marketing surveillance for long-term safety and rare adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease and chronic stable angina is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. His wife reports that he took a medication for erectile dysfunction earlier that evening. His blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, and he appears confused. Which of the following medications is most likely to have interacted with his erectile dysfunction drug, causing this severe hypotension?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Isosorbide dinitrate

 

The patient’s collapse and severe hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) after taking an erectile dysfunction (ED) medication (likely sildenafil) suggests a dangerous drug interaction with nitrates. Isosorbide dinitrate, a nitrate, is commonly used for angina and works by causing vasodilation. Sildenafil (PDE-5 inhibitor) also causes vasodilation by increasing cGMP levels.

 

When nitrates and sildenafil are taken together, they cause severe systemic vasodilation, leading to a profound drop in blood pressure, syncope, and even life-threatening shock.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clopidogrel: An antiplatelet drug used to prevent clot formation. It does not cause hypotension or interact with sildenafil.

 

Option B. Atorvastatin: A statin used for lipid control; does not cause hypotension or interact with sildenafil.

 

Option D. Metoprolol: A beta-blocker that can cause mild bradycardia and hypotension but does not have a severe interaction with sildenafil.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sildenafil is absolutely contraindicated in patients on nitrates due to the risk of life-threatening hypotension.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with bacterial meningitis is admitted to the hospital. The physician decides to start empirical therapy with a bactericidal antibiotic to ensure rapid bacterial eradication. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ceftriaxone

 

For serious infections like bacterial meningitis, a bactericidal antibiotic is preferred because it kills bacteria rather than just inhibiting their growth. Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, is bactericidal and commonly used in meningitis due to its good CSF penetration and broad-spectrum activity against common causative organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clindamycin: A bacteriostatic drug that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, mainly used for anaerobic infections and MRSA.

 

Option B. Linezolid: A bacteriostatic drug used against gram-positive bacteria like MRSA and VRE.

 

Option D. Doxycycline: A bacteriostatic tetracycline used for intracellular bacteria like Rickettsia and Chlamydia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bactericidal drugs like β-lactams (e.g., ceftriaxone) are preferred for serious infections like meningitis to rapidly clear the infection.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old HIV-positive male with a CD4 count of 180 cells/mm³ is started on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Two weeks later, he presents with complaints of vivid dreams, nightmares, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating, especially at night. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Efavirenz

 

One of the non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) is known to cause CNS side effects, including vivid dreams, nightmares, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating, particularly during the first few weeks of therapy. These symptoms often improve with time.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Abacavir: Can cause hypersensitivity reactions (HLA-B*5701 testing required) but not CNS toxicity.

 

Option C. Emtricitabine: Well-tolerated, with hyperpigmentation of palms/soles as a possible side effect.

 

Option D. Ritonavir: Used as a pharmacokinetic booster (CYP3A4 inhibitor), but does not cause CNS effects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Efavirenz is known for its CNS side effects, which typically improve over time and are more pronounced when taken close to bedtime.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old farmer presents with high-grade fever, headache, and myalgia for the past 7 days. On examination, he has generalized lymphadenopathy, a maculopapular rash on the trunk, and an eschar with surrounding erythema on his right thigh. His travel history reveals recent work in a forest area. Laboratory tests show thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following is the drug of choice for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Doxycycline

 

This patient’s presentation (fever, rash, eschar, thrombocytopenia, and recent travel to a forested area) is highly suggestive of scrub typhus, a rickettsial infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The drug of choice for rickettsial infections, including scrub typhus, is doxycycline.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Azithromycin: Can be used as an alternative in pregnant women or children, but doxycycline is preferred.

 

Option B. Ciprofloxacin: Not effective against rickettsial infections.

 

Option D. Ceftriaxone: Ineffective against rickettsial infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Doxycycline is the first-line treatment for scrub typhus and most rickettsial infections.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. He is currently on carvedilol, furosemide, and enalapril but continues to have dyspnea on exertion and fatigue. His physician decides to replace his ACE inhibitor with a newer drug that enhances natriuretic peptide activity and improves vasodilation and natriuresis. Which of the following drugs works through this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Sacubitril

 

The patient with HFrEF is being switched from an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) to a drug that enhances natriuretic peptides, suggesting Sacubitril. Sacubitril, used in combination with Valsartan as ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor), inhibits neprilysin, leading to increased BNP/ANP levels, causing vasodilation, natriuresis, and reduced cardiac remodeling.

 

Sacubitril is a neprilysin inhibitor, which increases natriuretic peptides and provides additional benefits in heart failure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Losartan: An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), does not inhibit neprilysin.

 

Option B. Ramipril: An ACE inhibitor, but ACE inhibitors are replaced by ARNIs in symptomatic HFrEF patients.

 

Option C. Aliskiren: A direct renin inhibitor, but renin inhibition does not enhance natriuretic peptides.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sacubitril (part of ARNI therapy) improves outcomes in HFrEF by inhibiting neprilysin, increasing natriuretic peptide levels, and reducing cardiac remodeling.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is started on an anticoagulant for long-term thromboprophylaxis. His physician prefers a drug that does not require routine coagulation monitoring for dose adjustments. Which of the following anticoagulants meets this criterion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dalteparin

 

Dalteparin, a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), has a predictable anticoagulant effect and does not require routine coagulation monitoring in most patients. Anti-Xa level monitoring is only needed in special populations (e.g., renal failure, obesity, pregnancy).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Warfarin: Requires INR monitoring due to variability in metabolism.

 

Option C. Unfractionated heparin: Requires aPTT monitoring for dose adjustments.

 

Option D. Argatroban: A direct thrombin inhibitor, requires aPTT monitoring, especially in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

 

Educational Objective:

 

LMWHs like dalteparin and enoxaparin do not require routine monitoring, making them preferable for outpatient anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation presents with chronic hypertension and requires antihypertensive therapy. She has a history of bronchial asthma and was recently diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nifedipine

 

All listed drugs are safe in pregnancy except Enalapril, which is contraindicated due to its risk of fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios, and congenital anomalies. Some other options are contraindicated due to the patient's comorbidities:

 

  • Methyldopa is avoided due to its association with hemolytic anemia (positive Coombs test).
  • Labetalol should be avoided in asthma due to its potential to cause bronchospasm.
    Thus, Nifedipine (a calcium channel blocker) is the safest choice in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Methyldopa: Safe in pregnancy, but contraindicated in hemolytic anemia due to risk of drug-induced hemolysis (Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia).

 

Option B. Labetalo: Safe in pregnancy, but contraindicated in asthma due to its beta-2 blocking effects, which can lead to bronchoconstriction.

 

Option C. Enalapril: Contraindicated in pregnancy as it is an ACE inhibitor, causing fetal renal damage and teratogenic effects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

ACE inhibitors like Enalapril are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa should be avoided in hemolytic anemia, and Labetalol should be avoided in asthma. Nifedipine is the preferred choice when these contraindications exist.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on multiple antipsychotic medications without significant improvement. His psychiatrist decides to start him on a drug that is known to be effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Three weeks after starting the medication, he develops fever, sore throat, and malaise. Laboratory investigations reveal a WBC count of 2,000/mm³ with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 800/mm³. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Clozapine

 

Clozapine is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. However, it has a serious side effect of agranulocytosis, which can present with fever, sore throat, and neutropenia. Due to this risk, regular monitoring of absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is required.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Risperidone: Can cause hyperprolactinemia, but does not cause agranulocytosis.

 

Option B. Olanzapine: Can cause metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes) but is not associated with severe neutropenia.

 

Option D. Quetiapine: Can cause sedation and hypotension, but not agranulocytosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Clozapine is highly effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia but requires frequent blood monitoring due to the risk of agranulocytosis. Regular ANC checks are mandatory to detect neutropenia early and prevent life-threatening infections.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation is admitted with preterm labor. To enhance fetal lung maturation and reduce the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), the obstetrician decides to administer a corticosteroid. Which of the following regimens is the most appropriate choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours for 48 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Methylprednisolone 16 mg IM once daily for 2 days

options.label: C
options.text: Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses

options.label: D
options.text: Dexamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses

questions.answerText: Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses

 

For fetal lung maturation in preterm labor (24–34 weeks gestation), corticosteroids like betamethasone or dexamethasone are administered to stimulate surfactant production, reducing neonatal RDS, intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis.

 

The recommended regimens are:

 

  • Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses (Correct answer)
  • Dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses (not the option given, but correct alternative)

 

In the question, Dexamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses (Option D) is incorrect because the correct regimen involves four doses of 6 mg each rather than two 12 mg doses.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours for 48 hours: Used for adrenal insufficiency, not for fetal lung maturation.

 

Option B. Methylprednisolone 16 mg IM once daily for 2 days: Does not cross the placenta effectively, making it ineffective for fetal lung maturation.

 

Option D. Dexamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses: Incorrect dosing regimen; correct regimen is 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For fetal lung maturation in preterm labor, the preferred corticosteroids are:

 

  • Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours (2 doses)
  • Dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours (4 doses)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old immunocompromised male with febrile neutropenia is diagnosed with disseminated mucormycosis. He is started on an antifungal agent that is drug of choice for this condition. What is the primary site of action of this drug?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cell membrane

 

Amphotericin B is a polyene antifungal that exerts its antifungal effect by binding to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, creating pores that increase membrane permeability, leading to leakage of intracellular contents and fungal cell death.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nucleic acid: Some antifungals like flucytosine act by interfering with fungal DNA/RNA synthesis, but amphotericin B does not.

 

Option B. Ribosome: Antibacterial agents like aminoglycosides act on ribosomes, but antifungals do not target this site.

 

Option D. Cytoplasm: Azoles like fluconazole inhibit ergosterol synthesis within the cytoplasm, but amphotericin B acts at the membrane level.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Amphotericin B acts on the fungal cell membrane by binding to ergosterol and forming pores, leading to fungal cell death. It is the drug of choice for life-threatening systemic fungal infections like mucormycosis and cryptococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis and a history of multiple fractures is prescribed a medication that acts without inhibiting osteoclast function. Which of the following drugs fits this mechanism of action?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Teriparatide

 

  • Teriparatide is a recombinant parathyroid hormone (PTH) analog that primarily activates osteoblasts to promote bone formation. 
  • Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab, or strontium ranelate, which inhibit osteoclasts, teriparatide does not inhibit osteoclast function, allowing balanced bone remodeling.
  • Works without inhibiting osteoclasts, instead promoting bone formation via osteoblast activation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Strontium ranelate: Inhibits osteoclasts and stimulates osteoblasts, but still has an anti-resorptive effect.

 

Option B. Ibandronate: A bisphosphonate that inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

 

Option D. Denosumab: A RANKL inhibitor that blocks osteoclast differentiation and function, leading to decreased bone resorption.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Teriparatide (PTH analog) is the only option that acts without directly inhibiting osteoclasts, making it suitable for osteoporosis treatment when bone formation needs to be enhanced.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic gout presents to the emergency department with sudden onset severe pain, redness, and swelling in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. On examination, the joint is tender, swollen, and warm, and the patient rates his pain as 9/10. You decide to start acute gout treatment. Which of the following is UNLIKELY to be the mechanism of action of the drug used in this setting?

options.label: D
options.text: Binds to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Inhibits synthesis of uric acid

 

  • Acute gout treatment focuses on reducing inflammation, not lowering uric acid levels.
  • NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin) work by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) to decrease prostaglandins and inflammation.
  • Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone) inhibit phospholipase A2, reducing inflammatory mediators.
  • Colchicine binds to tubulin, preventing neutrophil migration and reducing inflammation.
  • Uric acid-lowering drugs (e.g., allopurinol, febuxostat) act by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid synthesis, but are not used for acute attacks because they can worsen gout flares initially.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inhibits cyclooxygenase enzyme: NSAIDs act this way, making them a first-line choice for acute gout.

 

Option C. Inhibits phospholipase A2: Corticosteroids act this way, which are used in acute gout, especially when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

 

Option D. Binds to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration: Colchicine acts this way and is effective in acute gout treatment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids. Drugs that lower uric acid (allopurinol, febuxostat) are NOT used during an acute attack.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old male with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and recent myocardial infarction (MI) undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with stent placement. He is prescribed dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT)consisting of aspirin and ticagrelor to prevent stent thrombosis. Which of the following statements is true about ticagrelor?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an irreversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor

options.label: B
options.text: It is a pro-drug requiring hepatic activation

options.label: C
options.text: It has a faster onset of action than clopidogrel

options.label: D
options.text: It is affected by CYP2C19 inhibitors like omeprazole, reducing its efficacy

questions.answerText: It has a faster onset of action than clopidogrel
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It has a faster onset of action than clopidogrel

 

  • Ticagrelor is a direct and reversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor, unlike clopidogrel and prasugrel, which are irreversible.
  • Ticagrelor does not require hepatic activation, making it faster-acting than clopidogrel.
  • It is not a pro-drug, so its effect is more predictable and not affected by genetic variations in CYP2C19 metabolism.
  • Unlike clopidogrel, ticagrelor is not significantly affected by omeprazole or CYP2C19 inhibitors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is an irreversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor: Ticagrelor is a reversible P2Y12 inhibitor, unlike clopidogrel and prasugrel, which are irreversible.

 

Option B. It is a pro-drug requiring hepatic activation: Ticagrelor is an active drug and does not require hepatic activation.

 

Option D. It is affected by CYP2C19 inhibitors like omeprazole, reducing its efficacy: Unlike clopidogrel, ticagrelor is not significantly affected by CYP2C19 inhibitors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ticagrelor is a reversible, direct-acting P2Y12 inhibitor with a faster onset and more consistent action than clopidogrel, making it a preferred choice in ACS patients undergoing PCI.



erred choice in ACS patients undergoing PCI.

questions.stemHtml: A patient is administered Drug A, and its dose-response curve is plotted. Later, the patient receives Drug B or Drug C before administering Drug A again. The changes in the dose response curve are shown in the diagram below. Which of the following best describes the type of inhibition caused by Drug B and Drug C?

options.label: A
options.text: Drug B is a reversible competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is a non-competitive inhibitor

options.label: B
options.text: Drug B is an irreversible competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is a reversible competitive inhibitor

options.label: C
options.text: Drug B is a reversible competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is an irreversible competitive inhibitor

options.label: D
options.text: Drug B is a non-competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is an irreversible competitive inhibitor

questions.answerText: Drug B is a reversible competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is a non-competitive inhibitor
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Drug B is a reversible competitive inhibitor, and Drug C is a non-competitive inhibitor

 

The dose-response curve in the image shows the effects of Drug A alone and its modifications after pre-treatment with Drug B or Drug C.

 

Effect of Drug B (Green Curve Shift to the Right)

 

  • When Drug B is administered before Drug A, the dose-response curve shifts to the right, but the maximum effect (Emax) remains unchanged.
  • This suggests that higher doses of Drug A can overcome the inhibition, indicating reversible competitive inhibition.
  • Mechanism: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly to the active site of the receptor, preventing the agonist (Drug A) from binding. However, increasing the concentration of Drug A can outcompete the inhibitor.

 

Conclusion: Drug B is a reversible competitive inhibitor

 

Effect of Drug C (Red Curve: Decreased Emax)

 

  • When Drug C is administered before Drug A, the maximum effect (Emax) is reduced, but there is no significant shift in the EC50.
  • This suggests that inhibition cannot be overcome by increasing the dose of Drug A, which is characteristic of non-competitive inhibition.
  • Mechanism: Non-competitive inhibitors bind to an allosteric site (not the active site), altering receptor function in a way that reduces maximal efficacy without affecting drug binding affinity.

 

Conclusion: Drug C is a non-competitive inhibitor

questions.stem: A pediatric patient is brought to the emergency department with signs of ocular hypotension and apnea. The parents are concerned about the child's condition and have provided a history of recent medication use. It is crucial to determine which drug may have caused these symptoms in the infant. Drug capable of causing ocular hypotension with apnea in infants is: (NEET PG 2019)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Brimonidine

 

Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used to lower intraocular pressure in conditions such as glaucoma. It acts by decreasing the production of aqueous humor and increasing its outflow, thereby reducing intraocular pressure. While brimonidine is generally well-tolerated, it can have systemic side effects, particularly in infants. The most concerning systemic side effect in this context is central nervous system depression, which can manifest as symptoms like apnea (temporary cessation of breathing). Infants, especially premature ones, are more susceptible to such side effects. Therefore, brimonidine is the drug most likely responsible for causing ocular hypotension with apnea in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Timolol: Timolol is a beta-blocker commonly used to lower intraocular pressure. While it can have systemic side effects, including bradycardia and bronchospasm, it is not typically associated with apnea in infants.

 

Option C. Latanoprost: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog that lowers intraocular pressure by increasing the outflow of aqueous humor. It can cause side effects such as changes in iris color and eyelash growth. However, it is not known to cause apnea in infants.

 

Option D. Dorzolamide: Dorzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used in ophthalmology to reduce intraocular pressure. While it can cause ocular hypotension, it is not a common cause of apnea, especially in infants.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension is started on an anticoagulant to reduce his risk of stroke. He is prescribed an oral direct thrombin inhibitor that does not require routine INR monitoring. Unlike warfarin, this drug directly inhibits thrombin (factor IIa) and has a specific reversal agent available. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dabigatran

 

  • Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin (factor IIa) inhibitor used for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism (VTE) treatment.
  • Unlike warfarin, it does not require INR monitoring and has a specific reversal agent (Idarucizumab).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bivalirudin: Also a direct thrombin inhibitor, but it is given parenterally (IV), not orally.

 

Option C. Rivaroxaban: An oral factor Xa inhibitor, not a direct thrombin inhibitor.

 

Option D. Enoxaparin: A low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) that inhibits factor Xa, but it is administered subcutaneously, not orally.

 

Key Point: 

 

Dabigatran is the only oral direct thrombin inhibitor in routine clinical use.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child is found to be an asymptomatic carrier of Corynebacterium diphtheriae during a school health screening. He has no signs of pharyngitis or systemic illness. To prevent transmission to others, he is started on an antibiotic to eradicate the bacteria from his nasopharynx. What is the drug of choice for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Erythromycin

 

  • Erythromycin (oral or IM) is the drug of choice for eradicating the carrier state of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • Alternative: Penicillin G benzathine IM followed by Penicillin V orally for 10 days.
  • The goal of treatment in carriers is eliminating the bacteria to prevent transmission, even in asymptomatic individuals.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Amoxicillin: Not effective in eliminating C. diphtheriae carriers.

 

Option C. Rifampicin: Although it has activity against Corynebacterium diphtheriae, it is not the preferred choice for carrier eradication.

 

Option D. Tetracycline: Not used for diphtheria treatment or carrier state due to limited efficacy.

 

Key Point: 

 

Erythromycin for 7–10 days is the preferred regimen for diphtheria carriers.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of stable angina presents with complaints of exertional chest pain that is relieved by rest. His ECG and cardiac enzymes are normal. He is started on a drug that acts via a dual mechanism—by releasing nitric oxide (NO) and activating potassium (K⁺) channels, leading to coronary vasodilation and cardioprotective effects. Which of the following drugs has this dual mechanism of action?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Nicorandil

 

  • Nicorandil is a unique anti-anginal drug that works via a dual mechanism:
    1. Releases nitric oxide (NO) → Vasodilation via cGMP activation (like nitrates).
    2. Activates ATP-sensitive potassium (K⁺) channels (KCO) → Hyperpolarization and arterial vasodilation.
  • This dual action reduces myocardial oxygen demand and improves coronary blood flow, making it beneficial in angina and ischemic preconditioning.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ranolazine: Late sodium channel inhibitor, reduces intracellular calcium overload but does not activate K⁺ channels or release NO.

 

Option C. Trimetazidine: Metabolic modulator that shifts energy metabolism from fatty acid oxidation to glucose oxidation, reducing oxygen consumption but does not affect NO or K⁺ channels.

 

Option D. Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN): Releases NO, causing vasodilation, but does not activate K⁺ channels.

 

Key Point: 

 

Nicorandil is the only drug among the options that has both NO-releasing and K⁺ channel-opening properties, making it effective for angina management and ischemic preconditioning

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male undergoing chemotherapy for lung cancer develops severe vomiting on the third day after chemotherapy. He had mild nausea on the first day, which was controlled with medications. Now, despite taking oral antiemetics, he continues to have episodes of vomiting. Which of the following is the most effective drug for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Aprepitant

 

  • Aprepitant is a neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist that is specifically effective for chemotherapy-induced vomiting occurring after 24 hours (delayed phase).
  • The delayed vomiting typically starts after the first day (like on Day 2 or 3) and is not well controlled by 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (like Granisetron).
  • Aprepitant works by blocking substance P in the brain, preventing nausea and vomiting in the delayed phase.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Granisetron: A 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, highly effective for acute-phase vomiting (within 24 hours) but less effective for delayed vomiting. Many students may select this incorrectly!
 

Option C. Metoclopramide: A dopamine antagonist, useful in mild nausea but not the most effective for chemotherapy-induced vomiting.
 

Option D. Domperidone: Primarily a prokinetic drug, not very effective for chemotherapy-induced vomiting.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (Granisetron, Ondansetron) are commonly used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, delayed vomiting (after 24 hours) is best managed with NK1 receptor antagonists like Aprepitant.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with hospital-acquired pneumonia is started on a broad-spectrum antibiotic. However, this antibiotic is rapidly metabolized by renal dehydropeptidase-I, leading to its inactivation. To prevent this metabolism and prolong the drug’s action, Cilastatin is co-administered. Which of the following antibiotics requires Cilastatin for its efficacy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Imipenem

 

  • Imipenem is a carbapenem antibiotic that is rapidly degraded by renal dehydropeptidase-I (DHP-I) in the proximal tubules of the kidney.
  • Cilastatin is a DHP-I inhibitor, preventing the degradation of Imipenem and increasing its half-life and efficacy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Meropenem: Also a carbapenem but does not require Cilastatin, as it is resistant to renal dehydropeptidase.
 

Option C. Cefazolin: A first-generation cephalosporin, does not undergo significant renal metabolism.
 

Option D. Piperacillin: A β-lactam penicillin, often combined with Tazobactam (a β-lactamase inhibitor), but not affected by dehydropeptidase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cilastatin is always combined with Imipenem to prevent renal metabolism and improve its efficacy.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with breast cancer is undergoing chemotherapy and develops severe neutropenia. To stimulate neutrophil production, her oncologist prescribes pegylated-filgrastim instead of filgrastim. Which of the following is true about pegylated-filgrastim?

options.label: A
options.text: Duration of action is longer than filgrastim

options.label: C
options.text: It increases the risk of febrile neutropenia

questions.answerText: Duration of action is longer than filgrastim
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Duration of action is longer than filgrastim

 

  • Pegylated-filgrastim is a pegylated (polyethylene glycol-modified) form of filgrastim, a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) used to prevent neutropenia in chemotherapy patients.
  • PEGylation increases its half-life, reducing the need for daily dosing as seen with filgrastim.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. "It is a GM-CSF analog": Pegylated-filgrastim is a G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor), not a GM-CSF (granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor) analog. GM-CSF (e.g., sargramostim) stimulates both granulocytes and macrophages, while G-CSF mainly stimulates neutrophil production.

 

Option C. "It increases the risk of febrile neutropenia": Pegylated-filgrastim reduces the risk of febrile neutropenia and infections by promoting neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy.

 

Option D. "All of these are correct": Since B and C are incorrect, this option is also wrong.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pegylated-filgrastim has a longer duration of action than filgrastim, reducing the frequency of administration.

questions.stem: Osmotic diuretics, such as mannitol, work by increasing the osmolarity of plasma and renal tubular fluid, drawing water out of cells and into the intravascular space. This leads to increased urine output (diuresis). In which of the following conditions should intravenous mannitol be avoided?

options.label: C
options.text: Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to trauma

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Pulmonary edema

 

Mannitol initially expands intravascular volume before inducing diuresis. In patients with pulmonary edema, this fluid shift can exacerbate pulmonary congestion and worsen respiratory distress.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cerebral edema: Mannitol is used to reduce brain swelling by drawing excess fluid into circulation, lowering intracranial pressure.

 

Option B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Mannitol rapidly decreases intraocular pressure by pulling fluid from the eye into the bloodstream.

 

Option C. Raised ICP due to trauma: Mannitol is used in traumatic brain injury (TBI) to reduce brain swelling and ICP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mannitol is contraindicated in pulmonary edema and anuric renal failure due to the risk of fluid overload. However, it remains useful in neurological conditions like cerebral edema, raised ICP, and glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a long-standing history of bipolar disorder has been stable on lithium therapy. Recently, he was diagnosed with hypertension and started on thiazide diuretics. After a few days, he presented with coarse tremors and other symptoms suggestive of lithium toxicity. What is the likely mechanism of this interaction between lithium and thiazides? (NEET PG 2020)

options.label: A
options.text: Thiazide inhibits the metabolism of lithium

options.label: B
options.text: Thiazides act as an add-on drug to lithium

options.label: C
options.text: Thiazides increase the tubular resorption of lithium

options.label: D
options.text: Thiazides cause water loss thereby increasing lithium levels

questions.answerText: Thiazides increase the tubular resorption of lithium
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Thiazides increase the tubular resorption of lithium

 

Thiazides reduce the excretion of sodium in the renal tubules. Lithium is reabsorbed in a manner similar to sodium, leading to its increased reabsorption and elevated blood levels, resulting in potential toxicity. In this clinical case, the patient's symptoms of lithium toxicity are most likely due to the thiazide-induced increase in tubular reabsorption of lithium.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thiazide inhibits the metabolism of lithium: Lithium is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys, not metabolized. Thiazides don't affect lithium's metabolism.

 

Option B. Thiazides act as an add-on drug to lithium: There's no evidence that thiazides synergistically increase the toxic or therapeutic effects of lithium.

 

Option D. Thiazides cause water loss thereby increasing lithium levels: Thiazides do act as diuretics, but the primary mechanism of increasing lithium levels is through enhanced tubular reabsorption rather than water loss.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Thiazide diuretics increase the tubular reabsorption of lithium, leading to elevated blood levels and potential toxicity. This interaction is crucial to consider when prescribing thiazides to patients on lithium therapy.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis presents with complaints of fatigue, oral ulcers, and occasional nausea over the past few months. She has been on long-term treatment for her condition. Laboratory tests reveal macrocytic anemia. Liver function tests show mildly elevated transaminases. Which of the following drugs she might be taking is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Methotrexate

 

Methotrexate is commonly used for rheumatoid arthritis and can cause:

 

  • Stomatitis (oral ulcers)
  • Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)
  • Macrocytic anemia (due to folate antagonism)
  • Hepatotoxicity (elevated liver enzymes)
  • Bone marrow suppression and pulmonary toxicity (in severe cases)

     

Other Options:

 

Option A. Leflunomide: Causes hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy, but does not typically cause macrocytic anemia or stomatitis.

 

Option B. Chloroquine: Causes retinopathy, myopathy, and QT prolongation, but not macrocytic anemia.

 

Option D. Sulfasalazine: Can cause hemolytic anemia (especially in G6PD deficiency) and orange-colored urine, but macrocytosis is not a classic feature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Methotrexate toxicity is characterized by oral ulcers, nausea, macrocytic anemia, and hepatotoxicity.
  • Folic acid supplementation is essential to prevent these side effects.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with a history of bronchial asthma was recently started on an antipsychotic for schizophrenia. After a few days, he complains of severe restlessness, inability to sit still, and a strong urge to move his legs constantly, making it difficult for him to focus on daily activities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the patient that it will settle in a few days

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl)

 

Drug-induced akathisia is an extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) caused by antipsychotics, characterized by:

 

  • Inner restlessness
  • Inability to sit still
  • Constant leg movement, pacing

 

Management of Akathisia:

 

  • First-line: Beta-blockers (e.g., Propranolol)
  • Alternative: Anticholinergics (e.g., Benzhexol/Trihexyphenidyl) – especially preferred in asthma patientswhere beta-blockers are contraindicated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reassure the patient: Akathisia does not improve on its own and requires active treatment.

 

Option B. Increase the dose of antipsychotic: Worsens akathisia instead of treating it.

 

Option C. Propranolol: First-line for akathisia, but contraindicated in asthma due to risk of bronchospasm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Propranolol is the first-line treatment for akathisia, but in asthma patients, benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) is preferred.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and coronary artery disease has been on multiple medications, including metoprolol, atorvastatin, warfarin, amiodarone, and aspirin. He now presents with bluish-gray skin discoloration on sun-exposed areas. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Amiodarone

 

  • Amiodarone is known to cause photosensitivity and blue-gray skin discoloration, particularly on sun-exposed areas.
  • It occurs due to dermal deposition of amiodarone and its metabolites, and is more common with long-term use (>6 months) and higher doses (>400 mg/day).
  • Patients should be advised to use sunscreen and protective clothing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metoprolol: Can cause fatigue or bradycardia but does not lead to skin discoloration.


Option C. Atorvastatin: Can cause myopathy and liver dysfunction, but no bluish discoloration.


Option D. Warfarin: Can cause skin necrosis due to protein C deficiency but does not cause a blue-gray tint.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient on multiple drugs, amiodarone should be suspected if they develop blue-gray skin discoloration, especially on sun-exposed areas.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male is planning a trip to the mountainous region of Shimla. He has a history of motion sickness and is concerned about developing symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, and vomiting during the winding road journey. He visits his physician for advice on prophylactic medication. Which of the following drugs would be most appropriate for the prevention of motion sickness?

options.label: A
options.text: Acetazolamide oral tablet 250 mg twice daily

options.label: B
options.text: Scopolamine transdermal patch (apply 30 minutes before travel)

options.label: C
options.text: Promethazine oral tablet (take 30 minutes before travel)

options.label: D
options.text: Ondansetron oral tablet (take 30 minutes before travel)

questions.answerText: Promethazine oral tablet (take 30 minutes before travel)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Promethazine oral tablet (take 30 minutes before travel)

 

Promethazine is a first-generation antihistamine (H1-blocker) that is effective in preventing motion sickness by blocking histamine receptors in the vestibular system. It should be taken 30 minutes before travel for best results.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Scopolamine transdermal patch should actually be applied 12 hours before travel, not 30 minutes before. Applying it too late may reduce its effectiveness, leading to students choosing this incorrectly.

 

Option B. Acetazolamide is used for high-altitude sickness prevention, not motion sickness.


Option D. Ondansetron is a 5-HT₃ antagonist, mainly used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and not effective for motion sickness.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Many students may wrongly choose option B (Scopolamine patch 30 min before), but the correct answer is C (Promethazine 30 min before travel)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic heart failure (CHF) with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and hypertension was started on a new antihypertensive medication. A few days later, he developed a persistent dry coughwithout fever or dyspnea. His current medications include furosemide, carvedilol, spironolactone, and a recently introduced drug for heart failure. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Omapatrilat

 

  • Omapatrilat is a vasopeptidase inhibitor that inhibits both ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) and neprilysin.
  • Like ACE inhibitors, it increases bradykinin levels, leading to a persistent dry cough and a higher risk of angioedema.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Furosemide (Loop Diuretic): Causes electrolyte imbalances and dehydration, but not a dry cough.

 

Option B. Carvedilol (Beta-blocker): Can cause fatigue, bradycardia, and worsening CHF symptoms initially, but not cough.

 

Option C. Spironolactone (Aldosterone antagonist): Can cause hyperkalemia and gynecomastia, but not cough.

questions.stem: A patient on low dose aspirin therapy presented with occult blood in the stool. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this adverse effect?

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibition of thromboxane A2 synthase by aspirin

options.label: C
options.text: Gastric bleeding caused by aspirin to peptic ulcer

options.label: D
options.text: All of these. give answer and explanation

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Inhibition of Cyclooxygenase by Aspirin

 

Aspirin, even at low doses (75–150 mg/day), is associated with occult GI bleeding, but it does not directly cause peptic ulcers. Instead, its primary mechanism for GI bleeding is through inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX), particularly COX-1.

 

1. Low-dose aspirin does not cause peptic ulcers

 

  • Peptic ulcers are primarily caused by H. pylori infection and NSAIDs that significantly inhibit COX-1.
  • Low-dose aspirin is a weak acid and can cause mucosal injury, but it is less likely to induce deep ulcer formation compared to non-selective NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen).
  • However, low-dose aspirin can increase the risk of bleeding from pre-existing ulcers due to its antiplatelet effects.

 

2. Inhibition of Thromboxane A₂ Synthesis via COX Inhibition (Not TXA₂ Synthase Inhibition)

 

  • Aspirin does NOT inhibit thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂) synthase directly.
  • Instead, it irreversibly inhibits COX-1, which prevents the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H₂ (PGH₂), the precursor for thromboxane A₂.
  • TXA₂ synthase remains functional, but since its substrate (PGH₂) is depleted, TXA₂ production decreases, leading to impaired platelet aggregation and increased bleeding risk.

 

3. COX-1 Inhibition as the Main Cause of GI Bleeding

 

  • COX-1 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) in the gastric mucosa, leading to:
    • Decreased mucus and bicarbonate secretion
    • Increased gastric acid secretion
    • Mucosal injury and increased susceptibility to microbleeds
  • This explains why occult GI bleeding occurs even without ulcer formation in patients on low-dose aspirin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inhibition of thromboxane A₂ synthase by aspirin: Aspirin does not directly inhibit TXA₂ synthase; it only reduces the availability of its precursor (PGH₂)by inhibiting COX.

 

Option C. Gastric bleeding caused by aspirin due to peptic ulcer: Low-dose aspirin does not directly cause peptic ulcers but can exacerbate bleeding from pre-existing ulcers.

 

Option D. All of these: Since Option B and C are not entirely correct, the best answer remains A (COX inhibition).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Low-dose aspirin does not cause peptic ulcers but increases the risk of GI bleeding.
  • Aspirin inhibits COX, not thromboxane A₂ synthase.
  • COX-1 inhibition leads to decreased gastric protection and increased risk of occult bleeding.
  • Aspirin-induced GI bleeding can be reduced with PPIs (e.g., omeprazole) or enteric-coated formulations.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with lower back pain and a history of height loss over the past few years. She has a history of a Colles' fracture from a minor fall a year ago. A DEXA scan reveals a T-score of -3.0, confirming severe osteoporosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment for her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Alendronate (Bisphosphonate)

 

  • Alendronate, a bisphosphonate, is the first-line treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis, especially in those with a T-score ≤ -2.5 and a history of fragility fractures.
  • It inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, thereby improving bone mineral density (BMD) and reducing vertebral and hip fracture risks.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Denosumab: Used when bisphosphonates are contraindicated

 

  • A monoclonal antibody targeting RANKL, reducing osteoclast activity.
  • Preferred in patients with renal impairment or bisphosphonate intolerance.

 

Option B. Raloxifene: Not first-line, mainly used for vertebral fracture prevention

 

  • Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that mimics estrogen's effects on bones.
  • Reduces vertebral fractures but not hip fractures.

 

Option D. Calcitonin: Weak antiresorptive agent, not preferred

 

  • Provides short-term pain relief in acute vertebral fractures but is not a primary treatment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate, risedronate) are first-line therapy for osteoporosis.
  • Denosumab is an alternative for patients intolerant to bisphosphonates or with renal issues.
  • Raloxifene is mainly used for vertebral fractures, not hip fractures.
  • Calcium (1200 mg/day) and Vitamin D (800–1000 IU/day) supplementation is essential.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male patient was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate. The medication charts reveal that he was taking digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene. Suspecting the symptoms to be due to digoxin overdose, plasma levels of digoxin were ordered. It was found that his blood levels of digoxin have increased significantly. Which of his medications is most likely responsible for this increase in digoxin levels? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Clarithromycin.

 

  • Clarithromycin is known to inhibit the cytochrome P450 system, which is involved in the metabolism of many drugs, including digoxin. By inhibiting the metabolism of digoxin, clarithromycin can lead to elevated levels of digoxin in the blood, increasing the risk for digoxin toxicity.
  • Clarithromycin also acts as an inhibitor of the P-glycoprotein and can precipitate Digoxin toxicity. P glycoproteins are drug efflux pumps in the intestine that lead to a decrease in the bioavailability of drugs. Digoxin is one of the drugs that utilizes this mechanism for its metabolism. Therefore, the drugs which inhibit the Pgp can lead to the increased plasma concentration of Digoxin and lead to its toxicity.
  • Other drugs that inhibit the Pgp include 
    • Amiodarone
    • Verapamil
    • Diltiazem
    • Itraconazole
    • Propafenone
    • Flecainide 
    • Quinidine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Potassium chloride: This medication primarily affects potassium levels and has no significant interaction with digoxin metabolism.

 

Option C. Atenolol: Atenolol, a beta-blocker, is not known to significantly interact with digoxin metabolism.

 

Option D. Triamterene: This diuretic medication primarily affects sodium and potassium levels and is not known to have a significant impact on digoxin metabolism.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Clarithromycin can significantly increase plasma levels of digoxin by inhibiting its metabolism through the cytochrome P450 system and by inhibiting P-glycoprotein, leading to an increased risk of digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 4 presents with chronic lower back pain and asks for pain relief. Which of the following analgesics is the safest choice for long-term use in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acetaminophen (Paracetamol)

 

  • Acetaminophen is the safest analgesic for CKD patients because:
    • It is not nephrotoxic and does not impair renal perfusion.
    • It is metabolized in the liver, avoiding kidney overload.
    • It can be used for mild-to-moderate pain safely, even in CKD stage 4-5.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tramadol: Can be used but with caution

 

  • Metabolized in the liver, but its active metabolites are renally excreted.
  • Risk of accumulation in CKD → May cause seizures and respiratory depression.
  • Dose adjustment is needed in CKD (reduce dose and increase dosing interval).
  • Preferred over NSAIDs if stronger pain relief is needed.

 

Option B. Indomethacin & Option C. Diclofenac (NSAIDs): Contraindicated in CKD

 

  • Inhibit prostaglandins → Reduce renal perfusion → Can worsen CKD.
  • Increase risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) and electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalemia).
  • Should be avoided in all CKD patients, especially stage 3 or higher.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Acetaminophen is the safest choice for mild-to-moderate pain in CKD.
  • Tramadol can be used cautiously with dose adjustments.
  • NSAIDs (Indomethacin, Diclofenac) should be avoided in CKD.
  • If stronger pain relief is needed, opioids like tramadol (adjusted dose) or buprenorphine are preferred over NSAIDs.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis has persistent joint pain and swelling despite being on methotrexate. Her rheumatologist is considering adding anakinra to her treatment regimen. What is the mechanism of action of anakinra?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) IL-1 receptor antagonist

 

Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that blocks the action of interleukin-1 (IL-1) by competitively binding to the IL-1 receptor, preventing IL-1α and IL-1β from exerting their pro-inflammatory effects.

 

IL-1 plays a key role in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) by promoting:

 

  • Synovial inflammation
  • Cartilage degradation
  • Bone resorption

 

By blocking IL-1 signaling, anakinra reduces inflammation and joint damage in RA and is also used in auto-inflammatory syndromes like systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and adult-onset Still’s disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Inhibition of TNF-alpha:

 

  • TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab) block TNF signaling.
  • Anakinra does not target TNF-alpha.

 

Option C. Monoclonal antibody against IL-6:

 

  • Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets IL-6 receptors, not anakinra.

 

Option D. Extracellular increase in adenosine:

 

  • Methotrexate increases extracellular adenosine, leading to anti-inflammatory effects.
  • Anakinra works via IL-1 receptor antagonism, not adenosine modulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Anakinra is an IL-1 receptor antagonist, blocking IL-1 effects in inflammatory diseases.
  • Used in RA, Still’s disease, and auto-inflammatory syndromes.
  • Does not inhibit TNF-alpha, IL-6, or increase extracellular adenosine.
  • Less commonly used than TNF inhibitors but helpful in certain cases.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with obesity (BMI 34 kg/m²) and dyslipidemia visits the clinic for weight management. He is prescribed a drug that reduces dietary fat absorption in the intestine. Which of the following drugs is being referred to?

options.label: A
options.text: Ezetimibe, which inhibits NPC1L1 protein in the intestine to reduce cholesterol absorption

options.label: C
options.text: Liraglutide, which stimulates GLP-1 receptors to induce satiety

options.label: D
options.text: Tirzepatide which is dual agonist of GLP-1 and GIP

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Orlistat, which inhibits pancreatic lipase

 

  • Orlistat is a weight-loss drug that inhibits pancreatic lipase, preventing the breakdown and absorption of dietary fats in the intestine.
  • This leads to reduced fat absorption, thereby decreasing calorie intake and promoting weight loss.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ezetimibe: Incorrect (Common Confusion!)

 

  • Ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1 protein, blocking cholesterol absorption, not fat absorption.
  • Used for hypercholesterolemia, but does not cause significant weight loss.

 

Option C. Liraglutide: Incorrect

 

  • Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, promoting satiety and delayed gastric emptying.
  • Used for obesity and diabetes, but it does not block fat absorption like Orlistat.

 

Option D. Tirzepatide: Incorrect

 

  • Tirzepatide is a dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist that enhances insulin secretion, reduces appetite, and slows gastric emptying.
  • It promotes weight loss through appetite suppression, not by inhibiting fat absorption.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Orlistat inhibits pancreatic lipase → reduces fat absorption → aids in weight loss.
  • Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption but does NOT affect dietary fat.
  • Liraglutide & Tirzepatide help in weight loss via appetite suppression, not fat absorption inhibition.
  • Students may confuse Ezetimibe with Orlistat—both affect absorption, but one targets cholesterol, the other targets fat

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, excessive sweating, and glucose intolerance. MRI reveals a pituitary adenoma. The patient prefers an oral medication for treatment. Which of the following drugs is an oral agent used to treat acromegaly?

options.label: A
options.text: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog that inhibits GH secretion

options.label: B
options.text: Pegvisomant, a GH receptor antagonist that blocks GH action

options.label: C
options.text: Cabergoline, a dopamine agonist that suppresses GH secretion

questions.answerText: Cabergoline, a dopamine agonist that suppresses GH secretion
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cabergoline, a dopamine agonist that suppresses GH secretion

 

  • Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist that inhibits GH secretion, especially in acromegaly patients with coexisting elevated prolactin levels.
  • It is the only effective oral drug for acromegaly, although it is less potent than somatostatin analogs (Octreotide, Lanreotide).
  • Octreotide and Lanreotide are injectable somatostatin analogs, not oral drugs.
  • Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist, but it is administered subcutaneously, not orally.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient presented with rhinitis and swelling of the face. Intranasal biopsy revealed the presence of broad-based aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching. There was evidence of vascular invasion. What will be the preferred oral treatment for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Posaconazole

 

The patient has mucormycosis, a life-threatening fungal infection commonly seen in diabetic patients, especially with poorly controlled diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

 

Key features of mucormycosis:

 

  • Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement (rhinitis, facial swelling)
  • Broad-based, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching (histopathology)
  • Vascular invasion leading to tissue necrosis

 

Preferred treatment:

 

  • First-line (severe cases): Intravenous Amphotericin B
  • Oral step-down therapy: Posaconazole or Isavuconazole (used after stabilization)
  • Surgical debridement is crucial to remove necrotic tissue

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caspofungin: Incorrect

 

  • Echinocandins (Caspofungin, Micafungin, Anidulafungin) are ineffective against Mucorales.
  • They target β-glucan synthesis, but Mucorales have low β-glucan content in their cell walls.

 

Option B. Amphotericin B: Incorrect (Not Oral Form)

 

  • Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for severe mucormycosis but is only available in IV form.
  • Oral amphotericin B is not available for mucormycosis treatment.

 

Option D. Terbinafine: Incorrect

  • Terbinafine is effective against dermatophytes (e.g., tinea infections), not Mucorales.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • IV Amphotericin B = First-line for mucormycosis
  • Posaconazole or Isavuconazole = Oral step-down therapy
  • Echinocandins (Caspofungin) & Terbinafine are ineffective
  • Surgical debridement is essential
